t: Minimum Time Takes to Reach Destination Without Drowning
o: Two simultaneous processes: water spreads one ring per second from all '*' cells (multi-source BFS), and the person moves one cell per second from 'S' to 'D'. A cell is enterable at time t only if it isn't stone and its flood time exceeds t (stepping onto a cell flooding at the same instant kills you). Precompute floodTime[i][j] with one multi-source BFS over '.' cells, then run a second BFS for the person, expanding to a neighbor only if floodTime > currentTime+1. 'D' never floods, so reaching it is safe. Example 1 gives 3 seconds; Example 2 shows the water wall sealing off D → −1. Grid ≤ 100×100, so two BFS passes at O(nm) are trivially fast.
k: Precompute flood times with multi-source BFS from all '*' cells.
Person's BFS expands to a neighbor only if floodTime[neighbor] > dist[current]+1 (strict inequality handles same-second drowning).

a.n: Approach 1: Two-Pass BFS (Flood Times, Then Person)
a.i: Pass 1 computes the earliest time each open cell floods. Pass 2 runs BFS from S; a neighbor is enqueued when unvisited, not stone, and its flood time is strictly greater than the arrival time. Return dist[D] or −1.
s: Multi-source BFS from all '*' across '.' cells to fill floodTime (stones and S/D excluded).
BFS from S; relax neighbors with floodTime[x][y] > dist[cur]+1.
Return dist at D, or −1 if unreachable.
a.t: O(n·m) — two linear BFS passes over the grid

a.i: Instead of precomputing flood times, advance water one level and the person one level alternately each second: expand all water cells, then expand all person cells, checking against freshly flooded cells. Same complexity; useful when memory for a separate flood grid should be avoided or when simulating visually.
s: Keep a water frontier and a person frontier.
Each second: expand water frontier into '.' cells; then expand person frontier into cells not stone, not visited, not water now or previously.
Stop when D reached or person frontier empties.
a.t: O(n·m) — each cell processed a constant number of times

w: Prefer Approach 1 for clarity; the strict inequality flood > arrival is the crux — stepping onto a cell at the exact moment it floods is fatal. Note water does not spread through S, X, or D cells (only '.'), and D is guaranteed safe. Pitfall: mutating the grid in Approach 2 destroys input for repeated calls — copy if needed. Follow-up: multiple people, or water spreading diagonally.
